title: Breastfeeding: Getting Off to a Good Start
hook: A deep latch is the foundation of comfortable, effective breastfeeding — and most early hurdles like soreness and engorgement settle once attachment and supply find their rhythm.
key_points: A good latch is key: bring baby to the breast nose-to-nipple so they take a big mouthful, not just the nipple tip.
Feed often and on demand — newborns may want the breast very frequently, even hourly in the early days.
Supply responds to demand: the more your baby feeds, the more milk your body makes.
Sore nipples and engorgement are common early on and usually settle as attachment improves; ask for lactation help early if it hurts.
content_html: Breastfeeding is a skill that you and your baby learn together, and the thing that makes it click is a good latch. The NHS advises bringing your baby to the breast — not the breast to the baby — with their nose level with your nipple so they tip their head back and open wide, taking a big mouthful rather than just the nipple tip. When attachment is good, your baby's chin touches the breast, their cheeks stay rounded, and you can hear them swallowing.
extra_html: Feed often and on demand: in the first days newborns may want the breast very frequently, even close to every hour, and that frequent feeding is exactly what builds your supply, which works on demand — the more your baby feeds, the more milk your body makes. Early hurdles like sore nipples or engorgement are common and usually settle as the latch improves. The NHS encourages reaching out early if feeding hurts: a midwife, health visitor, or breastfeeding supporter can check the latch in person. This is general guidance; a lactation consultant or your health visitor can help with your specific situation.

related.title: Breastfeeding and Formula Both Feed a Baby Well
related.hook: Health bodies recommend breastfeeding where possible, but properly prepared infant formula is a safe, nourishing alternative — a fed baby is the goal.

related.title: Feeding on Demand: Cues and How Often
related.hook: Newborns feed best on demand — watch for early hunger cues rather than the clock, and let wet and dirty diapers, not the exact count of feeds, reassure you they're getting enough.

related.title: Why Breastfed Babies Need Vitamin D Drops
related.hook: Breast milk is nearly perfect — but it's low in vitamin D. Pediatricians recommend a daily 400 IU vitamin D supplement for every breastfed and partly breastfed baby, starting in the first days.

flashcards.prompt: What's the single most important thing for comfortable, effective breastfeeding?

choices.text: A good, deep latch — baby takes a big mouthful, not just the nipple tip
Feeding strictly every 4 hours on a clock

flashcards.explanation_html: The NHS emphasizes bringing baby to the breast nose-to-nipple so they take a large mouthful. A deep latch is the foundation of effective, comfortable feeding.

flashcards.prompt: How does your body decide how much milk to make?

choices.text: Supply responds to demand — more feeding signals more milk
Supply is fixed at birth and can't change
Supply depends only on how much water you drink

flashcards.explanation_html: Milk production works on supply and demand: the more your baby feeds, the more milk your body makes.

flashcards.prompt: Are sore nipples and engorgement in the first days a sign you should stop?
flashcards.back_html: No. They're common early hurdles that usually settle as attachment improves. If feeding hurts, ask for lactation help early rather than waiting it out.
